name: Manguissa (canton Ebombo)
overview: The Ebombo canton, twelve Manguissa villages, lives in harmony with the Engba grouping, the Begnia Bega, the people of the Sanaga and the Saa canton, and welcomes Hausa, people from Bamenda, Bamiléké and Malians. Having come, like the other Beti, from the other bank of the Sanaga, the Manguissa grow cocoa, groundnut and cucumber and every year initiate their young people into the minken mimbon dance.

sections.title: Identity and neighbours
items: A vast canton of 12 villages, which has long demanded its own arrondissement.
Manguissa (leti) is spoken there, also present in Mbam-et-Kim.
Very extended kinship; the canton is a mixture of many groups (Hausa, people from Bamenda, Bamileke, Malians).

sections.title: Territory and migrations
items: The Manguissa crossed the Sanaga on the back of the snake, then stayed at Okola; they remain linked to the Bavek and the Mvog Manga.
The mbon, instrument and symbol, represents the man who has come through the hardest trials: the Manguissa is very attached to tradition.

sections.title: Social organisation and power
items: The king (canton chief) governs Ebombo; modern politics (fianga) is now what divides people.
In case of misfortune, the chief gathers patriarchs and notables, then the whole canton, where everyone gives their opinion.
A married and worthy man (ati) has a say; an unmarried man can hardly speak before the elders.
Today alliances and divisions follow political affiliations; initiation has lost importance with the missions.
The wife owes respect to her husband; children learn good manners.

sections.title: Kinship, marriage and life passages
items: Kinship both matrilineal and patrilineal; the woman joins her husband.
People marry from the age of 18; each family makes enquiries about the other, and a rite (megornd) purifies families that have been through hardship.
Steps: meeting of the betrothed, meeting of the families, “knocking at the door”, handing over of the list and bride price, then civil marriage, very important.
Bride price: kolas, palm wine, snuff (nsoan) for the mothers, pigs, goats, which signify alliance and acceptance.

sections.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos
items: Rites: nvole nnam to bless the village (elders and sages), mbappi for the sick, rites for childless women, mbon to obtain boys in the clan.
Symbolic places: the chiefdom, the tomb of a great chief (who keeps his wisdom), the Mboso'o river, the abegle ma tree, whose creaking announces misfortune.
Birth is the return of a forebear and a happiness, which is greeted by bringing kola nuts; the dead send warnings.
Taboos: a pregnant woman does not eat palm rat; children do not eat snake; a woman does not wash her feet outdoors.
Serious offences: incest, adultery, relations with one's father's or uncle's wife; the chief imposes a sentence served within the group.
In case of difficulty, the chief consults the village elders.

sections.title: Economy, land and crafts
items: Cocoa planters; groundnut, cucumber, sweet potato and cassava crops.
The land falls under the State; the canton does not sell land, land is inherited.
Crafts: trays (metamkere), drying racks (itang), raphia beds and chairs, hoes, pottery (kouli, jar for cool water).

sections.title: Clothing, health, beauty
items: Chiefs and notables wear the ebom (hat, bag), wrapper, démembré, fly whisk; initiates dance the mbon dressed in the obom. Women, formerly in loincloths, today wear the kaba.
People gladly treat themselves with plants.
Beauty: the man who is a good speaker, well-groomed, able to provide for his family; the woman with natural hair, beautiful curves, without artifice, a good cook.
Courtship: cleanliness and hard work, for both sexes.

sections.title: Music, dances and festivals
items: Rhythms: bikutsi, minken mimbon (specific to the Manguissa), minkul; instruments: bell, tam-tam of great mourning, balafon.
Dances: kam (shaking of the shoulders, shared with the Eton), minken mimbon, essani for the deceased who left an admirable legacy.
Festival: the great annual gathering of the canton, where young people are initiated into the minken mimbon dance.

sections.title: History and cultural kinship
items: The Manguissa have authority without liking to impose it; they live in community and resemble the Eton and the Ewondo.

sections.title: The names
items: Formerly, some names were exclusively feminine (Ngono, Ngah); names of robust animals are readily given (Zogo, “strength”).
A name may be changed once if it brings bad luck.
One starts with the family name; tone changes the meaning: Ateba pronounced “Atoa” means “seated”.
The founding ancestor, Ateba Noah Molo, is a name shared with the Eton.

lessons.title: Who are the Manguissa (canton Ebombo)? Identity, language and territory
objectives: Name the Manguissa (canton Ebombo) community and explain its name
Locating your territory and its neighbours
Telling one's origin according to tradition

vocabulary.frenchText: Cry of surprise (due to the coolness of the water)

lessons.competence: Introduce the Manguissa (canton Ebombo) community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within the cultural diversity of Cameroon.
lessons.situation: A pen pal from another region asks you to introduce the Manguissa (canton Ebombo) community to them: who are they, where do they live, where do they come from?
lessons.materiel: Map of Cameroon, cultural profile of the community (“Cultures” section of Likalo).

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Present the Manguissa (canton Ebombo) community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within Cameroon's cultural diversity.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A pen friend from another region asks you to introduce the Manguissa (canton Ebombo) community to them: who are they, where do they live, where do they come from?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What do the Manguissa (canton Ebombo) call themselves and what does this name mean? — What language do they speak, and where else is it spoken? — Which peoples do they live with? — Where did they come from, according to tradition?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • A vast canton of 12 villages, which has long demanded its own arrondissement. • Manguissa (leti) is spoken there, also present in the Mbam-et-Kim. • Very extended kinship; the canton is a mix of many groups (Hausa, people from Bamenda, Bamiléké, Malians). • The Manguissa crossed the Sanaga on the back of the serpent, then stayed at Okola; they remain linked to the Bavek and the Mvog Manga. • The mbon, instrument and symbol, represents the man who has come through the hardest trials: the Manguissa are very attached to tradition.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: The Ebombo canton, twelve Manguissa villages, lives in harmony with the Engba grouping, the Begnia Bega, the people of the Sanaga and the Saa canton, and welcomes Hausa, people from Bamenda, Bamiléké and Malians. Having come, like the other Beti, from the other bank of the Sanaga, the Manguissa grow cocoa, groundnut and cucumber and every year initiate their young people into the minken mimbon dance.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: On a map of Cameroon, locate the Manguissa (canton Ebombo) community and its neighbours, then write 5 sentences to introduce it to your pen pal.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.title: Power and social organisation among the Manguissa (canton Ebombo)
lessons.anelcac: Socio-political organisation, rules for living together
lessons.competence: Describe how the Manguissa (canton Ebombo) organise power, make decisions and regulate community life.
lessons.situation: An important decision must be made for the whole Manguissa (canton Ebombo) village. Who decides, and how?
lessons.materiel: The community's cultural profile, paper and felt-tip pens for the organisation chart.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “An important decision has to be made for the whole Manguissa (canton Ebombo) village. Who decides, and how?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — Who holds authority? — How are decisions made (consensus, vote, the chief's decision)? — What rules of respect and deference are observed? — Which groups or societies play a particular role?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)

objectives: Linking food to the living environment

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the main dishes and drinks? — What products are they made from? Where do these products come from? — Who prepares them, and on what occasions? — What do they say about the community's living environment?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Traditional dishes: okok, ntchenkè (okra leaves and nuts), sesame sauce. • Drinks: palm wine, ha'a, arki (spirits). • Cocoa planters; groundnut, cucumber, sweet potato and cassava farming.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: The Manguissa (canton Ebombo) mainly eat okok, ntchenkè, sesame sauce. Traditional drinks: palm wine, ha'a, arki. These dishes are linked to the group's activities and to the products of its environment.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Describe the stages of the traditional Manguissa (canton Ebombo) marriage, the elements of the bride price and their symbolism.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “Your older brother wants to marry a young Manguissa (canton Ebombo) woman. Which steps will he have to follow?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — Who chooses the spouse? Do people marry within the group or outside it? — What are the stages of marriage? — What does the bride price include, and what does each item symbolise? — Where does the couple live after the marriage?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following points: • Kinship both matrilineal and patrilineal; the woman joins her husband. • People marry from 18; each family finds out about the other, and a rite (megornd) purifies families that have suffered hardship. • Stages: meeting of the fiancés, meeting of the families, “knocking at the door”, handing over the list and bride price, then civil marriage, which is very important. • Bride price: kola nuts, palm wine, snuff (nsoan) for the mothers, pigs, goats, which signify alliance and acceptance.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Steps: meeting of the betrothed, meeting of the families, “knocking at the door”, handing over of the list and bride price, then civil marriage, very important. Bride price: colas, palm wine, snuff (nsoan) for the mothers, pigs, goats, which signify the alliance and the acceptance.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: In a group, act out a marriage proposal among the Manguissa (canton Ebombo), then explain the meaning of two elements of the bride price.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-IV — Cultural practices in communities (Level I)
lessons.title: Leisure: traditional music and dances of the Manguissa (canton Ebombo)
objectives: Describe a dance and its instruments
lessons.competence: Identify the traditional dances of the Manguissa (canton Ebombo), choose the most representative one, describe it, bring out its cultural significance and act it out.
lessons.situation: Taking part in cultural life in the family and in society: the class prepares a Manguissa (canton Ebombo) dance performance for the cultural day.
lessons.materiel: Instruments or recordings, costumes, clear space.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Identify the traditional dances of the Manguissa (canton Ebombo), choose the most representative one, describe it, bring out its cultural significance and perform it.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “Taking part in cultural life in the family and in society: the class is preparing a Manguissa (canton Ebombo) dance performance for cultural day.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — Which dances are practised, and on what occasions? — Who dances (men, women, children, initiates)? When and where? — Which instruments, songs and outfits are used? — What is the cultural meaning of the chosen dance?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following points: • Rhythms: bikutsi, minken mimbon (specific to the Manguissa), minkul; instruments: bell, tam-tam of great funerals, balafon. • Dances: kam (shaking of the shoulders, shared with the Eton), minken mimbon, essani for the deceased who left an admirable legacy. • Festival: the great annual gathering of the canton, where young people are initiated into the minken mimbon dance.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Among the Manguissa (canton Ebombo), traditional dances (shoulders, minken mimbon, funerals) accompany the major moments of life: festivals, mourning, weddings, initiations. Instruments: mbon, bell, drum, balafon. Festival(s): annual gathering of the Ebombo canton.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Describe a Manguissa (canton Ebombo) dance (participants, time, instruments, gestures, meaning), then perform it with your group.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-IV — Cultural practices in communities (Level I)
lessons.title: Traditional economy and access to land among the Manguissa (canton Ebombo)
lessons.competence: Describe the economic activities of the Manguissa (canton Ebombo), the division of tasks between men and women and the rules of access to land.
lessons.situation: A development project wants to help the Manguissa (canton Ebombo). First it must understand how they work and who owns the land.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Describe the economic activities of the Manguissa (canton Ebombo), the division of tasks between men and women and the rules of access to land.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A development project wants to help the Manguissa (canton Ebombo). First it must understand how they work and who owns the land.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the activities of men? of women? — Who owns the land and how is it accessed? — Which products are sold or exchanged? — Have these activities changed?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following points: • Cocoa planters; crops of groundnut, cucumber, sweet potato and cassava. • Land belongs to the State; the canton does not sell land, land is inherited. • Crafts: trays (metamkere), drying racks (itang), raffia beds and chairs, hoes, pottery (kouli, a jar for cool water).

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Cocoa planters; groundnut, cucumber, sweet potato and cassava crops. Land belongs to the State; the canton does not sell land, land is inherited.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Draw a two-column table (men / women) of the Manguissa (canton Ebombo)'s activities, then explain how land is accessed.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos among the Manguissa (canton Ebombo)
objectives: Explain beliefs about life and death

vocabulary.langText: rat palmiste pour la femme enceinte

lessons.competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Manguissa (canton Ebombo), and their role in regulating social life.
lessons.situation: A visitor arrives among the Manguissa (canton Ebombo). Which places and which rules must he absolutely respect?

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Manguissa (canton Ebombo), and their role in regulating social life.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A visitor arrives among the Manguissa (canton Ebombo). Which places and which rules must they absolutely respect?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the beliefs about birth and death? — Which places are sacred, and why? — What are the main taboos, and for whom? — How were serious offences atoned for?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following points: • Rites: nvole nnam to bless the village (elders and sages), mbappi for the sick, rites for childless women, mbon to obtain boys in the clan. • Symbolic places: the chiefdom, the tomb of a great chief (who keeps his wisdom), the Mboso'o river, the abegle ma tree, whose cracking announces misfortune. • Birth is the return of an ancestor and a happiness, which is greeted by bringing kola nuts; the dead send warnings. • Prohibitions: a pregnant woman does not eat palm rat; children do not eat snake; a woman does not wash her feet outside. • Serious offences: incest, adultery, relations with one's father's or uncle's wife; the chief imposes a penalty served within the group.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Rites: nvole nnam to bless the village (elders and sages), mbappi for the sick, rites for childless women, mbon to obtain boys in the clan. Symbolic places: the chiefdom, the tomb of a great chief (which keeps his wisdom), the Mboso'o river, the abegle ma tree, whose creaking announces a misfortune.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Write a short guide to good conduct for a visitor among the Manguissa (canton Ebombo) (3 places or rules to respect, with their reason).

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Greeting, introducing yourself and counting in Manguissa
lessons.anelcac: Traditional media and transmission: everyday language
objectives: Greeting according to the time of day

vocabulary.langText: Mekoni woah Me vasse koni woah

vocabulary.frenchText: morning greetings (as a sign of deference/respect)

lessons.competence: Use the greeting and introduction formulas of the Manguissa (canton Ebombo) and count from 1 to 10, respecting customs.
lessons.situation: You are visiting a Manguissa (canton Ebombo) family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of kola nuts by counting.
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile (“Common expressions” and “Counting” sections), kola nuts or small objects.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Use the Manguissa (canton Ebombo) greeting and introduction formulas and count from 1 to 10, respecting customary usage.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “You are visiting a Manguissa (canton Ebombo) family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of the cola nuts by counting.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — How do you greet people depending on the time of day? — How do you introduce yourself (name, origin, place of residence)? — How do you count from 1 to 10? Is the system decimal, vigesimal…? — Why is language a tool of transmission?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following points, or have the students discover them: • The community's language is Manguissa. • Greeting formulae: Mekoni woah Me vasse koni woah = Hello (neutral greeting, at any time of day); Mbembe kekidi = morning greeting (one person); Mekoni min kéhh oo = morning greeting (several people). • Counting from 1 to 5: Po’og, Ba’a, Laal, Na’a, Tan. • The founding ancestor, Ateba Noah Molo, is a name shared with the Eton. • The Manguissa has authority without liking to impose; he lives in community and resembles the Eton and the Ewondo.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Greeting and counting in Manguissa are the first steps towards communicating with the Manguissa (canton Ebombo). The polite expressions convey the respect owed to people according to the time of day and their rank.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Role play in pairs: greet each other, introduce yourselves, ask where the other person comes from and count objects from 1 to 10.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.
